blocks.text: "You always did love junk," my sister Brenda sneered as she handed me a cardboard box of Mom's old kitchen jars.

We were standing in the driveway of Mom's house two days after the funeral. Brenda had already changed the locks on the back door. The will had been read that morning at Mr. Halvorsen's office: Brenda got the house and $145,000 in savings, my brother Gary got the thirty-eight acres of family land, and I received twelve chipped ceramic jars shaped like farm animals.
I didn't argue. I just took the box and put it in the trunk of my Honda.

I'd spent the last four years caring for Mom while Brenda and Gary barely visited. When Mom's heart started failing and she couldn't drive anymore, I was the one who left my bookkeeping job in Toledo, moved into a small rental five minutes from her house, and handled every doctor's visit, every pill organizer, and every middle-of-the-night fall.

Brenda lived forty minutes away and came by maybe four times a year, usually around holidays, staying just long enough to complain about the clutter in the hallway. Gary lived in Indiana and called on Sundays for ten minutes while watching football.

I was fifty-eight years old, my own savings were down to a few thousand dollars, and my back still hurt from lifting Mom out of the bathtub two months ago. Still, I didn't fight them in the driveway. I was too tired, and honestly, I'd spent most of my life letting Brenda have the louder voice so we wouldn't have a scene.

That night, in my quiet kitchen, I unpacked the box and started washing the jars one by one in warm soapy water. They were dusty from sitting on top of Mom's oak cabinets for twenty years. A rooster with a chipped beak.
A spotted cow. A little sheep whose glaze had crazed with age. I dried each one and lined them up on a towel on the counter.
Then I picked up the heavy pig-shaped jar.
It felt strangely off-balance, heavier on one side than the others. When I tilted it under the faucet, something slid inside and bumped the ceramic wall.
I turned off the tap, dried my hands on my apron, and pried the tight rubber-ringed lid open. My hands stopped right there over the sink.

Stuffed into the bottom was an old blue-and-white striped dishcloth I remembered from when I was a girl. I pulled it out. Hidden beneath the dishcloth was a thick manila envelope folded in half, sealed with masking tape, with my name written on the front in Mom's shaky blue ballpoint pen: "For Claire."
I sat down at my kitchen table with my wet sleeves still rolled up and peeled off the masking tape.

Inside were two things. The first was a stamped bank form from Heartland Credit Union, dated eighteen months earlier. It was a Payable on Death beneficiary designation for Mom's savings account, listing the balance at the time and naming me, Claire Miller, as the sole beneficiary of the $145,000.
The second was a single sheet of lined notebook paper folded around the form.

"Claire," Mom had written. "If you are reading this, Brenda gave you the jars like I knew she would. I did not change the old will because I am too tired to watch your sister and brother tear you apart in probate court and claim you pressured me. They already think they know what is theirs. Take this paper and my death certificate to Heartland Credit Union on Monday morning before Brenda goes in waving that will. The lady at the desk told me this form comes first.
You gave me four years of your life. Do not let them talk you out of it."

I read the letter three times under the humming kitchen light. For four years, I had wondered if Mom even noticed how much I was giving up while Brenda and Gary stayed away. Now I knew she had seen every bit of it.
I looked at the clock on the microwave. It was eleven-thirty on a Saturday night. Brenda had told me at the funeral that she was taking Monday off work to "start sorting out the bank stuff."
I had thirty-six hours before my sister walked into that credit union.

Sunday afternoon, I caught myself reaching for my phone twice to call Brenda and tell her what I'd found. That was my old habit kicking in, the part of me that always wanted to smooth things over before a fight could start.
Maybe if I explained it nicely, I thought, we could talk it through like adults.

Then I looked at the pig jar sitting on my counter and remembered the week Mom had pneumonia two winters ago. I'd called Brenda at ten at night because I was running a fever myself and couldn't lift Mom to the bathroom. Brenda had told me she had an early meeting and hung up. Gary hadn't answered at all.

Monday morning at nine o'clock sharp, I was standing at the counter of Heartland Credit Union. I'd brought my driver's license, the stamped POD form, Mom's letter, and one of the certified copies of her death certificate.

I only had the death certificate because I was the one who had sat with the funeral director and paid the deposit out of my own checking account while Brenda and Gary argued over whether to order lilies or roses.

A branch representative named Denise took my paperwork into a back office for ten minutes. My palms were sweating the whole time. I kept thinking there had to be a catch, that Mom's signature wouldn't match or the old will would somehow cancel it out.
When Denise came back out, she sat down across from me and smiled gently.
"Everything is in order, Ms. Miller," she said. "A Payable on Death designation passes outside the will. It doesn't go through probate."
She turned her monitor slightly so I could see the account summary. The balance, with eighteen months of modest interest, was $146,210.40.

Denise explained that they would close Mom's account and transfer the funds into a new savings account in my name, though it would take two business days for the internal transfer to settle completely. I signed three forms, thanked her, and walked out to my Honda with my knees shaking.
I didn't hear a word from Brenda until Tuesday afternoon at four-fifteen.
I was folding laundry when my phone rang. Her name flashed on the screen. I let it ring twice, then answered.
"What did you do?" she said. Her voice was tight and high.
"Don't play dumb with me, Claire. I just left Heartland Credit Union. I brought the will and the executor papers, and they told me the savings account is closed. Closed! Where is the $145,000?"
"It wasn't part of the estate," I said, keeping my voice steady even though my heart was hammering against my ribs.
"Mom put me down as the Payable on Death beneficiary a year and a half ago."
There was a sharp intake of breath on the other end. "You drove her down there," Brenda snapped. "You snuck her into that bank when she was sick and made her sign that!"

"I didn't even know she did it until Saturday night," I said. "She hid the copy in the pig jar you gave me. And Mom was sharp as a tack eighteen months ago, Brenda. You'd know that if you'd come by more than twice that year."
"You're a thief," she yelled. "I'm calling Gary, and I'm calling Halvorsen. You won't keep a dime of that money."
She hung up. Ten minutes later, Gary called.
I didn't answer, so he left a voicemail telling me I'd crossed a line and that they were going to haul me into court for taking advantage of a sick old woman.

I sat on the edge of my couch listening to his message, and for a second that familiar knot formed in my stomach. Part of me wanted to offer them half just to make the yelling stop. Then I walked into the kitchen, picked up Mom's letter from the table, and read the last line again.

Wednesday morning, before Brenda and Gary could corner me, I paid $250 out of my checking account for a one-hour consultation with a local elder law and estate attorney named Richard Vance. I wanted to know the truth from someone who didn't care about our family drama.
I showed him the will, the POD copy from the credit union, and Mom's handwritten letter.

Mr. Vance read through everything carefully and took off his glasses. "In this state, a properly executed POD designation supersedes a will," he told me. "It's a direct contract between your mother and the credit union. As long as she was competent when she signed it eighteen months ago, they have no legal claim to it."
"My brother threatened to sue me for undue influence," I said.
"People threaten that a lot," he said plainly. "To win, they'd have to prove you isolated her and forced her hand. Were you in the room when she signed it?"
"No. I think she must have gone in while I was across the street picking up her prescriptions at Walgreens. I used to drop her at the credit union door so she wouldn't have to walk far."
"Then they'd be spending ten or fifteen thousand dollars in legal fees on a case they'll almost certainly lose. Keep your copies safe, and don't argue with them over the phone."
That evening at six o'clock, headlights pulled into my driveway. Through the living room blinds, I saw Brenda's white SUV, with Gary's pickup truck right behind it.
I unlocked the front door and stepped onto the small porch before they could start pounding on it.
Brenda came up the steps first, holding a folded manila folder with the will inside. Gary stayed a step behind her, his jaw set.
"Let's go inside," Brenda said. "We need to talk."
"We can talk right here," I said. "My neighbors don't care."
Brenda glared at me, then held up the will. "The will says the savings are mine, Claire.
You know Mom meant for that money to go with the house to pay the taxes and upkeep. You need to go back to that credit union tomorrow and sign it over to the estate."
Gary stepped forward. "Come on, Claire. Don't make this ugly. We're family. If we have to take this to a judge, it's going to cost all of us."

"I already spoke to an estate lawyer this morning, Gary," I said calmly. "A Payable on Death account doesn't go through probate. Mom signed it herself eighteen months ago. Her doctor's records from that year show she was completely clear-headed, and I wasn't even in the building."
